author: Brian Hioe
title: Animal Rights Advocates Call for Referendum on Snare Traps
content:
ANIMAL RIGHTS ADVOCATES are currently campaigning for a referendum to be held on the use of wild boar snares.

In particular, animal rights advocates have long criticized wild boar snares as overly cruel. Such traps use spring-loaded mechanisms to tighten around animals’ limbs when triggered.

Nevertheless, such traps have also been criticized for ensnaring other species, as they do not distinguish. Endangered species such as Formosan black bears and leopard cats had also been killed by such traps, as have cats and dogs, sometimes resulting in their losing limbs if they survive.

Though claims had been made that Indigenous hunters used such traps as part of traditional hunting rights, animal rights groups have generally cited that this was rarely the case, in that Indigenous hunters generally do not use such traps. By contrast, such animal rights advocates state that Indigenous hunters more commonly use traps made from wood, bamboo and vines, and other natural materials. In the past, the Central Election Commission turned down calls for a referendum on the use of wild boar snares on the basis that the referendum was unclear as to whether it pertained to traps used by Indigenous hunters.

Otherwise, such traps are sometimes used by farmers as a means of preventing damage to their crops. Animal rights advocates have called on the government to provide electric fencing, protective

author: Brian Hioe
title: In A First, China Sanctions Ministers of Diplomatic Allies of Taiwan
content:
THE CHINESE GOVERNMENT has sanctioned two government ministers from diplomatic allies of Taiwan. These would be Belizean Foreign Minister Francis Fonseca and Paraguayan Minister of Information Gustavo Villate. Such sanctions prevent them and their family members from doing business in China.

China does not appear to have sanctioned ministers of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies in the past. This would be a new means, then, of pressuring countries to switch ties from Taiwan to China.

Taiwan is larger than all of its diplomatic allies, whether measured in terms of the size of population or economy. The main reason why Taiwan maintains ties with its diplomatic allies is so that they can speak up for it in international organizations in which Taiwan is not a member.

That being said, Taiwan has also long been accused of “dollar diplomacy”–paying off diplomatic allies through infrastructure investment deals or slush money to high-ranking politicians in return for recognition. Indeed, one notes that many of Taiwan’s diplomatic allies are countries that have questionable human rights records.

Though China offers much the same to such allies in return for switching recognition, Taiwan is unable to outspend China. China is, of course, much larger than Taiwan. Likewise, small states risk being shut ouf of the lucrative–and much larger–Chinese market if they retain ties with Taiwan.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Army Suicide Reminds of Recurring Issues with Bullying and Hazing in the Military
content:
A RECENT CASE in which a female Army first lieutenant committed suicide is being investigated as a potential case of bullying. The first lieutenant in question, surnamed Wang, jumped to her death from a building at the Army’s 206th Brigade base in Hsinchu County on September 30th. An audio recording that was posted on Threads on October 12th shows a man berating Wang for failing to heed instructions, leading to the bullying allegations.

The Ministry of National Defense has vowed that the case is being investigated and that Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo is attentive to its developments. This would not be the only case in recent years in which a suicide in the military has been linked to bullying.

In November 2020, a similar case emerged of a corporal surnamed Liu stationed in the Eighth Army Command’s 203rd Brigade in Danei District, Tainan, who died by hanging. Liu, too, was reportedly bullied by his superiors and peers.

The most famous case of a death in the military thought to have resulted from bullying in the military would be the death of cadet Hung Chung-chiu in July 2013. Hung is thought to have been bullied by his superiors and peers shortly before his discharge from mandatory military service, as a form of hazing or as retribution against him before his service ended. author: Brian Hioe
title: Delivery Workers Criticize Plans by Grab to Acquire Foodpanda
content:
DELIVERY WORKERS from the National Delivery Workers’ Union demonstrated outside the Fair Trade Commission (FTC) earlier this month against plans by Grab to acquire Foodpanda. Specifically, delivery workers have criticized that the acquisition of Foodpanda by Grab would create monopoly conditions that would be detrimental to workers’ rights.

Taiwan’s food delivery landscape is already a duopoly between Foodpanda and Uber. Uber holds 13% of shares in Grab. Likewise, previously Uber sought to acquire Foodpanda in a deal that was blocked by the Fair Trade Commission. As such, Uber is accused of potentially seeking to acquire Foodpanda through a different means.

At the time, the National Food Delivery Workers’ Union called for the FTC to investigate the impact of the deal on workers’ and consumers’ rights, as well as the impact of what a monopoly would be. Namely, Uber Eats and Foodpanda were already criticized in the past as unilaterally raising costs for workers and prices for consumers, and the former’s acquisition of the latter may make this problem more severe.

Nevertheless, one notes that Grab has also been criticized over potential links to China. Consequently, members of the National Delivery Workers’ Union were joined by the Economic Democracy Union and DPP politicians such as Wang Shih-chien and Kao Chia-yu. author: Brian Hioe
title: Taiwan Again Rolls Out the Red Carpet for an Authoritarian Monarch For National Day
content:
KING MSWATI III of Eswatini was recently in Taiwan for National Day. As a result, the red carpet was once again rolled out for the authoritarian monarch, who presides over Africa’s last absolute monarchy, by the Lai administration.

In particular, apart from Mswati III’s presence at National Day, President Lai Ching-te and Mswati III visited Taiwan’s Air Force Command. Lai touted support from Mswati III on establishing the Taiwan Industrial Innovation Park, as well as Eswatini’s role as Taiwan’s gateway into Africa. Eswatini is Taiwan’s only remaining diplomatic ally in Africa.

Ties between Eswatini and the Lai administration have been in the spotlight in recent years, especially after a dramatic visit to the country by Lai. In May, a planned trip by the Taiwanese president for King Mswati III’s 58th birthday and the 40th anniversary of his accession to the throne was abruptly canceled.

This occurred because countries that Lai would have passed over on his flight to Eswatini, Madagascar, Mauritius, and the Seychelles revoked overflight permissions shortly before Lai was to set out. This was largely interpreted as China flexing its muscles in terms of its influence in Africa, with the Lai administration suggesting that China threatened to revoke debt cancellation for Madagascar, Mauritius, and the Seychelles if they did not comply.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Why Would Chiang Wan-an Propose Replacing Songshan Airport with an “AI Park”?
content:
IN AN UNUSUAL proposal, Taipei mayor Chiang Wan-an has proposed replacing Songshan Airport with an AI park. Chiang claims that this AI park would involve not only technological facilities, but also greenery and residential areas.

This is not the first time such a proposal has been made. In the past, DPP political candidates such as Lee Ying-yuan in 2002, Frank Hsieh in 2006, and Enoch Wu in 2022 have made similar proposals to move Songshan Airport and to replace it with a park.

Nevertheless, the central government has rejected such proposals in the past, citing security concerns. High-level officials usually travel from Taiwan to other countries through Songshan Airport, as do foreign dignitaries. Songshan Airport also serves some functions for the Taiwanese military, as it is guarded by it because of the view that the Chinese military would seek to capture it in the event of an invasion. Located in downtown Taipei, Songshan Airport is the smaller airport that serves Taipei besides Taoyuan International Airport. Unlike Taoyuan International Airport, it is located inside the city rather than outside of it.

Flights to Taiwan’s outlying islands are usually serviced outside of Songshan Airport. In recent years, short-range flights to Japan and South Korea have also operated from Songshan Airport. Indeed, it is hard to imagine that residents of Taiwan’s outlying islands would be

author: Brian Hioe
title: Lai Plays It Safe Ahead of Elections in National Day Address
content:
LAI’S NATIONAL DAY address this year largely played it safe. Lai did not introduce any new major proposals, but emphasized that his administration would maintain its existing stances. Notably, Lai could have leaned into attacks on the KMT ahead of elections in November but did not.

Lai began by emphasizing national unity. Lai stated that despite differences in backgrounds, political views, and generations, Taiwan should be united by a responsibility to protect Taiwan and its future. Lai raised, then, that Taiwan recently saw the 30th anniversary of direct presidential elections.

Lai, then, went on to emphasize Taiwan’s resilience in a turbulent international world. The world has seen continued conflict, as well as tariff shocks, but Lai framed Taiwan as remaining committed to non-red supply chains, and becoming part of the foundation of the international order. In this sense, Lai emphasized strengthening ties between Taiwan and its allies, whether that be Eswatini, Palau, or Europe, though, of course, one notes that Eswatini is an authoritarian monarchy. King Mswati III of Eswatini was present at National Day celebrations this year in person.

Lai said that Taiwan should seek to be a “city on a hill” in providing a model for the world.

Lai touted Taiwan’s strong economic performance, along with the accomplishments of its athletes, as signs of Taiwan’s resilience. Nevertheles

author: Brian Hioe
title: Lai Administration Raises Minimum Wage, But Not Likely to Correct Structural Inequalities
content:
THE MINIMUM WAGE Deliberation Committee announced late last month that the minimum wage will be increased from 29,500 NT to 30,900 NT. This will mean an hourly increase in the minimum wage from 196 NT to 205 NT. The change is expected to impact 2.61 million people, including 414,400 migrant workers.

It is not surprising that the minimum wage has been increased. It is, after all, election year. It is unlikely that the Lai administration would decline to increase the minimum wage when nine-in-one elections are to occur in two months. Likewise, the increase pushes the minimum wage over 30,000 NT for the first time, which the DPP can tout as a triumph.

At the same time, one notes that certain professions in Taiwan see increasingly fewer individuals willing to take them. Around 10% of convenience stores, for example, have been found to no longer be operating 24/7, due to a labor shortage.

This labor shortage has resulted in blue-collar migrants taking up such professions. Without formal avenues outside the legally established professions in fishing, as caretakers, forestry and agriculture, or in factories, blue-collar work has instead occurred through what are legally internships, even if the government has made some moves to further regulate such internships as it would other forms of blue-collar work, and some flagship programs have been rolled out in order to allow migrant wor

author: Brian Hioe
title: Xindian Eviction Case Illustrates Recurrent Dynamics
content:
A FORCED EVICTION case in Xindian has drawn concern from Taiwanese civil society, with long-term residents of a historic structure possibly forced to vacate it in the near future.

In particular, the eviction case revolves around the Tsai Jin-mu house, which has been inhabited by the Lai family for eighty years and was built by their grandfather, Tsai Jin-mu. The Lai family previously sought to seek cultural preservation status for the structure, as an example of architecture that dated to the Japanese colonial period. However, this was denied by the Cultural Bureau of the New Taipei City government in June, which concluded that the bricks used in the structure are similar in size to those that date from the Japanese colonial period, but that this could not prove that the structure indeed dated from then.

Other structures in the neighborhood have already been demolished, starting from 2006, because of the construction of the Liugong Canal. Nevertheless, the Lai family was unexpectedly sued in 2014, demanding the return of the land, having found out that the Irrigation Association had sold the land in 2012 to a developer for a low price without notifying. Although the Lai family had expressed a desire to purchase the land 60 years prior, at the time, the Irrigation Association had claimed that the land was government property that was hard to deal with.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Indigenous Groups Protest Typhoon Ragasa Response Last Month
content:
INDIGENOUS COMMUNITY members protested last month outside of the Executive Yuan, marking the one-year anniversary of deadly flooding in Matai’an, also known as Guangfu Township. The deadly flooding occurred after Typhoon Ragasa in September 2025.

Such community members have called on the Executive Yuan to ensure that reconstruction is carried out in coordination with the wishes of the local community, while working with the local government to do so. On the other hand, community members have criticized when reconstruction takes place in such a manner that leads to mass land expropriation, depriving local residents of their land.

In this sense, Matai’an community members have criticized broken promises from the government, which has promised to fund reconstruction and provide resources. The protest also raises how Matai’an has become highly dependent on donations from the outside world after the deadly flooding.

As part of the demonstration, participants threw plastic bottles filled with sand and water from Matai’an at photos of KMT caucus leader Fu Kun-chi, Hualien county magistrate Hsu Cheng-wei, Ljaucu Zingrur, head of the Council of Indigenous Peoples, and minister without portfolio Chen Chin-te.

author: Brian Hioe
title: What Did China Intend to Accomplish Through Surveilling Lai Ching-te’s Son?
content:
THE FBI HAS arrested a woman, Wanying “Heather” Zhang, for acting as an unregistered foreign agent of China. In particular, Zhang’s arrest occurred because she was apparently conducting surveillance on Lai Ting-yu, the son of President Lai Ching-te.

Lai’s family generally keeps a low public profile. Lai, who is in his 30s, is thought to work for electronics manufacturer Philips and to have a young child. Zhang is accused of traveling to Seattle from Los Angeles and renting a vehicle to surveil Lai’s home along with an accomplice.

Zhang is accused of being in contact with a Chinese handler through WeChat, as well as other individuals she knew were Chinese government officials. Zhang worked as a real estate agent and was detained as she was about to board a flight for Shanghai. It is possible, then, that Zhang could be a civilian recruited by China, or that the Chinese government has continued with its practice of employing “disposable” agents.

It is unclear what China hoped to gain from surveilling Lai, who was not likely to have any sensitive government information. Nevertheless, one aim could be to threaten, by putting Lai and his family members living abroad on edge, and to warn of the potential repercussions of going against China. author: Girard Mariano Lopez
title: Taipei Gay Bar Raid Sparks Protest, Scrutiny Of City’s Commitments to LGBTQ+ Rights
content:
A POLICE RAID on a longstanding gay bar in Taipei sparked a lightning protest and demands for independent oversight after patrons alleged humiliation and discrimination, prompting disciplinary action against officers and an apology from the mayor weeks before the city’s annual Pride celebrations.

About 100 to 200 people gathered at 1 p.m. Oct. 4 outside a police substation near Red House, a landmark in Taipei’s LGBTQ+ district. After speeches, demonstrators marched through the busy neighborhood to the Ximending Police Station which reportedly dispatched the order to raid the gay bar, demanding an explanation and apology for the previous afternoon’s operation at Commander D.

The dispute has drawn scrutiny of police treatment of sexual minorities and intensified questions about whether Taipei’s promotion of LGBTQ+ inclusion abroad is reflected in its policing at home.

Officers entered the BDSM-themed bar Oct. 3 with what police described as a court-issued search warrant obtained under prosecutors’ supervision following complaints about suspected sexual offenses. Police said the establishment had received 13 complaints this year.

Authorities said 51 people were referred for suspected violations of the Social Order Maintenance Act and the operator for a suspected criminal offense. That account differed from protest speakers’ figure of 59 people taken for questioning.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Recent Incidents Highlight Chinese Transnational Repression in Taiwan
content:
A NUMBER OF recent incidents illustrate new tactics in China’s playbook for transnational repression.

For one, a comedy club in Taipei–known as Comedy Club or Comedy Plus +–had its entrance smeared with a mixture of feces and white paint. It is thought that this occurred due to performances by comedian Huang Yi-hao. Huang previously mocked Chinese president Xi Jinping during a stand-up routine in December 2025, clips of which recently went viral online.

A 35-year-old man surnamed Kuo was reportedly paid 50,000 NT by a 33-year-old man surnamed Liu to carry out the attack. It is unclear whether the two were acting at China’s behest.

Past similar incidents include when Hong Kong pro-democracy singer Denise Ho and bookstore owner and publisher Lam Wing-kee, one of the Causeway Bay booksellers, were splashed with red paint by attackers. Some of these attackers were linked to Taiwanese pro-China organized crime groups such as the Bamboo Union gang.

Likewise, Aegis, a restaurant that assisted Hongkongers seeking refuge in Taiwan, and a gym owned by a pro-democracy Hongkonger who had previously stood as an electoral candidate, had faced similar incidents. Aegis was splashed with chicken feces by men who were paid by a Chinese national to carry out the act.

The gym in question was splashed with red paint by two individuals who arrived from Hong Kong. The two individuals departed ba

author: Brian Hioe
title: KMT Presses Ahead With Efforts to Legalize Caning
content:
THE KMT HAS signaled that it intends to press ahead with efforts to institutionalize caning as a punishment for severe crimes. Such crimes would include sexual assault, child abuse, driving under the influence of drugs, and serious cases of fraud.

Previously, the KMT intended to push for a national referendum to be held on caning as a punishment for such crimes. The KMT did not plan to campaign with the general public in order to hold a referendum on caning, however. Instead, the KMT simply pushed through the referendum using its current majority in the legislature.

As such, it is a question whether the referendum would catch on with the general public. There was no previous demand for caning to be instituted as a punishment in Taiwan, even if capital punishment is known to be highly popular with the general public as a punishment against violent crimes, with the view that it is an effective deterrent against violent crimes in society.

In the past, the KMT has attempted to frame a 2024 decision by the Constitutional Court that narrowed the scope of capital punishment but kept it on the books as a de facto abolition of capital punishment. In response, the KMT called for national referendums on capital punishment. Though such referendums were thrown out by the Central Election Commission for not being factual, the KMT would be attempting to use referendums in order to benefit

author: Brian Hioe
title: Kaiser Kuo’s “The Great Reckoning” Proves a Mass of Banal Truisms Playing on Western Insecurities
content:
KAISER KUO’S “The Great Reckoning: What the West Should Learn From China” is something less than an argument. It is instead a number of disconnected gestures, intended to cast doubt upon Western hegemony and suggest the ascent of China as an alternative to the US-led global order.

Indeed, Kuo denies that his argument is a claim that China’s system is superior, but that “it is instead a call for the kind of frank, sober assessment that genuine confidence requires”. This is merely intellectual camouflage for what is, of course, a claim that the Chinese system is superior–and an attempt to paper away its authoritarian aspects through the invocation of culturalism. The easiest way to claim that the Chinese system is superior, in fact, is through the claim to not do that.

But, in this, the argumentation is largely tautological–it starts from the a priori assumption that China is something qualitatively different than the West, then sets out to demonstrate this point it already assumes. That this facile gesture has caught on at all speaks more to those who seek to promote this banal attempt at intellectualism; intellectualism with its pants off more than anything else.

Rather amusingly, Kuo begins by invoking Adam Tooze, who joins a long-storied lineage of Western Orientalists with the claim that “China isn’t just an analytical problem. [It is] the master key to understanding mode

author: Brian Hioe
title: Taiwanese Continue to Be Detained in China After the End of Their Formal Sentences
content:
TAIWANESE ACADEMIC Tsai Chin-shu has returned to Taiwan, nearly eight years after his arrest in China. Tsai was the head of the Southern Taiwan Union of Cross-strait Relations Associations and director of the Kaohsiung Cross-Strait Exchanges Research Association. Tsai also held a Ph. D from Xiamen University’s Graduate Institute for Taiwan Studies, one of China’s major research centers about Taiwan. Tsai’s return was made known by a post by him on social media earlier this month.

In his capacity as head of these organizations, Tsai was, in fact, apparently an advocate of political unification between Taiwan and China. The Southern Taiwan Union of Cross-strait Relations Associations advocates closer political and economic relations between Taiwan and China and was a supporter of the Ma administration’s efforts at establishing closer ties with China, as observed in the organization’s support of the 2015 Ma-Xi meeting.

Tsai was detained on charges of endangering Chinese state security and was detained by Chinese authorities in July 2018 after crossing into Xiamen, China from Kinmen in order to attend a cross-strait food fair. As has happened with many other cases of cross-strait detentions, Tsai’s family kept quiet, but that he had been detained by Chinese authorities was revealed by Shih Chien University professor Chiang Min-chin, a member of the KMT, who disclosed information

author: Brian Hioe
title: Does the Trump-Xi Meeting Show the Outcome of Over-Reliance on the US?
content:
THE TRUMP-XI MEETING that took place in Washington DC over the weekend largely proved to be a non-event. Relatively little of consequence was remarked upon by the two leaders, except the two sides committing to reduce tariffs on some 30 billion USD worth of goods.

If Taiwan hoped to keep out of the limelight, one notes that in the course of the meeting, Xi Jinping did seek to convince the US of historical ties between the two countries–even if the “China” that Xi referred to was actually the Republic of China, rather than the People’s Republic of China. Trump himself claimed that the two leaders had not spent much time discussing Taiwan.

What proved more of a curveball, however, was later comments to Fox News by US ambassador to China, David Perdue, who stated that Trump had offered to sell US arms to China in the course of their conversation. Perdue claimed that this was not the first time that Trump had made such comments to Xi before and that this had come up before past meetings. Nevertheless, Perdue also emphasized that US policy on Taiwan remained unchanged. Trump now denies that this ever took place.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Does China Intend to Target Taiwan With New National Security Legislation?
content:
TAIWANESE GOVERNMENT officials, speaking under conditions of anonymity to the media, have warned that China may roll out national security legislation directed at Taiwan in the coming months. Such national security legislation would follow up on China’s recently passed ethnic unity law.

The law criminalizes actions aimed at disrupting a vaguely defined “national unity”. Although initial warnings were that the law was mainly aimed at Tibetans and Uyghurs, the Lai administration has framed such national security legislation as potentially a threat to Taiwan. Under such laws, after all, support for Taiwanese independence–or even just maintaining Taiwan’s current democratic freedoms and its de facto independence–could be construed as illegal and criminal under the law.

Such Taiwanese government officials have pointed to a number of laws, some of which are still in the review process, as potentially impacting Taiwan. This includes the Regulations of the State Council on Exit and Entry Administration, Measures for the Supervision and Inspection of Cyberspace Security, and National Defense Mobilization Law.

author: Brian Hioe
title: Why Did the KMT Reverse Course on Drone Spending?
content:
AFTER MUCH political contention about the budget earlier this year–including Taiwan’s defense spending–the KMT eventually relented and passed the national budget after over 200 days of stalling at the end of last month. Though the KMT had originally proposed cutting or freezing drone spending–in fact, suggesting that it might cut or freeze all budget that would have been allocated to drones, this did not come to pass.

The KMT seemed to have suddenly become aware of the poor optics of blocking drone spending after an article in The Economist, which lashed out at the KMT as obstructionist and self-interested for continuing to block drone spending when this could be vital to Taiwan’s defense against Chinese threats. In short order, then, the KMT legislative caucus suddenly had a reversal of course.

Nevertheless, the KMT’s approval of drone funding places this under the central government budget, rather than as a special budget. The original special expenditure for drone spending that the Lai administration originally hoped to pass was 210 billion NT for three specific drone systems, which would have been unmanned aerial vehicles and maritime drones.

The 240 billion NT passed by the KMT was for all military drone spending, not just those specific three systems, and annual spending would be capped at 40 billion NT. 31 billion was originally budgeted by the military for unmanned s

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will There Be Increased Discussion of Climate Resilience in Taiwan?
content:
A RECENT ARTICLE in the New York Times ranked Taipei lowest out of the 72 cities that it assessed in terms of climate preparedness. In the wake of the article, the two Taipei mayoral candidates–Puma Shen of the DPP and Chiang Wan-an of the KMT–have traded barbs on what it would take to make Taipei more prepared. Chiang largely attempted to play up the accomplishments of his mayoral administration to date, while Shen has called for proactive measures.

Indeed, there has not been much discussion to date of climate preparedness in Taiwan. The particularities of the Taiwanese political context have led much discussion about environmentalism to be confined to discussing Taiwan’s energy mix, with the issue of nuclear energy remaining contentious.

The issue of nuclear waste storage has long been controversial, in that Taiwan has a limited land mass, as a result of which local communities end up being foisted with nuclear waste storage facilities. The impact of the 2011 Tohoku typhoon and tsunami led to increased consideration in Taiwan of what could occur if there were a catastrophic tsunami or earthquake, such as led to the meltdown of the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear reactor.

On the other hand, discussion of the suitability or unsuitability of Taiwan for nuclear energy has largely cleaved along partisan lines in past decades. In more recent times, however, the DPP has reversed course

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will Kuai Kuai Workers Strike?
content:
WORKERS AT ONE of Taiwan’s best-known snack companies, Kuai Kuai, have voted in favor of a strike.

The strike authorization takes place after an announcement by the company that it would be selling the land on which its existing factory sits on in Zhongli and moving to Hsinchu. The two sites are 39 kilometers from each other, meaning that the move is untenable for many workers.

In particular, workers were only informed of the land scale on September 1st. According to the Ministry of Labor, the move was not expected for another two years. The factory has operated in Zhongli since 1968, and 1/3rd of workers at Kuai Kuai have worked there for more than thirty years, despite the fact that their wages are near minimum wage.

The land sale is ironic. Namely, the land will be sold to Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc. At a time when the semiconductor sector is dominant, as fueled by the AI boom, this has led to significant land acquisitions by semiconductor companies.

Yet Kuai Kuai is an iconic snack in the technology industry. Namely, it is a common superstition in Taiwan that bags of Kuai Kuai can prevent machines and equipment from malfunctioning. It is ironic that Kuai Kuai workers are being thrown under the bus by the very industry the snack is associated with.

author: Yo-Ling Chen
title: Dear Sherry: A Daybreak Digital Memorial
content:
The following letter serves as a digital memorial to Sherry Yue (she/they; 邱梓榳 Chiu Zi Ting, known affectionately as 玥餅 Yuèbǐng by her friends), who died by suicide on April 16, 2026 at the age of 26. It is written by one of Sherry’s friends and fellow trans activists, Yo-Ling Chen, a contributing editor at New Bloom who worked with Sherry and an early iteration of the Trif Trans Bar team to establish Taiwan’s first trans bar in New Bloom’s events/community space, Daybreak (破曉咖啡). Sherry was a minimalist, vegetarian, front-end engineer who enjoyed reverse-engineering things for fun, and someone who loved life with an adventurous passion the year before her departure.

I am so, so sorry that I missed your funeral…

I know that you wouldn’t want to see me beating myself up over this, and I also know that you would have appreciated the various kinds of work I was buried under that led to the insomnia, which led to me mixing up the funeral time, which led to me arriving to an empty ceremony hall at the exact moment your body was in the final stages of cremation. I rushed to the crematorium hoping that I would at least see a part of you one last time—a single wisp of smoke from the chimney, that would have been enough. But that’s not how modern crematoriums work.

Don’t worry, I’m not actually beating myself up over this. I am, however, thinking about you, our friendship, ways to ho

author: Brian Hioe
title: Will New Changes Improve Taiwan’s Image on Migrant Work?
content:
A NUMBER OF changes are set to occur in the migrant work landscape in Taiwan going forward.

For one, the first batch of migrant workers in the hospitality field has arrived, consisting of 35 Indonesians. These 35 workers arrived in Taiwan as part of the new Multinational Skilled Worker Enhancement Program and are classified as skilled labor, rather than blue-collar migrant workers. The 35 workers previously conducted internships in Taiwan of at least one year in length and are required to reach A-2 level listening and speaking within three years, per the requirements of the program.

Their employer, Regent Taipei, previously hired them as interns, and it approached them individually under the new program. The 35 workers are mostly in their twenties and will return to the departments they worked in. The terms of the new program specify that hospitality industry businesses can hire a new migrant worker if they increase the salary of their lowest-paid Taiwanese worker by 2,000 NT, though hiring of migrant workers is still capped at 10% of the workforce.

The hospitality industry, which has a shortfall of 6,000 workers annually, has long clamored for hiring migrant workers to take up positions that Taiwanese are no longer interested in working.
